claim: CVD is responsible for about a third of both human and captive chimpanzee deaths.
source: CVD is responsible for about a third of both human and captive chimpanzee deaths (WHO; Varki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to WHO and Varki et al., 2009

claim: The anatomy of the healthy human and chimpanzee heart is similar.
source: The anatomy of the healthy human and chimpanzee heart is similar; however CVD pathology differs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Chimpanzee CVD is often associated with interstitial myocardial fibrosis.
source: Chimpanzee disease is often associated with interstitial myocardial fibrosis, while human heart disease predominantly results from coronary artery artherosclerosis, leading to ischemic damage (Lammey et al., 2008; Varki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lammey et al., 2008 and Varki et al., 2009

claim: Human heart disease predominantly results from coronary artery atherosclerosis, leading to ischemic damage.
source: Chimpanzee disease is often associated with interstitial myocardial fibrosis, while human heart disease predominantly results from coronary artery artherosclerosis, leading to ischemic damage (Lammey et al., 2008; Varki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lammey et al., 2008 and Varki et al., 2009

claim: Interstitial fibrosis etiology is the most frequently diagnosed form of CVD in captive bonobos, gorillas and orangutans.
source: The interstitial fibrosis etiology prevalent in chimpanzees is also the most frequently diagnosed form of CVD in captive bonobos, gorillas and orangutans (Lowenstine et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowenstine et al., 2016

claim: The heart is the most oxygen-demanding tissue in the body.
source: The heart is the most oxygen-demanding tissue in the body (Giordano, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giordano, 2005

claim: 20–40 min of oxygen deprivation results in irreparable damage to the human heart.
source: Indeed, 20–40 min of oxygen deprivation results in irreparable damage to the human heart (Bretschneider et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bretschneider et al., 1975

claim: The electrophysiology of mouse cardiomyocytes differs substantially from that of human cardiomyocytes.
source: In addition to genome-level differences between humans and mice, the electrophysiology of mouse cardiomyocytes differs substantially from that of human cardiomyocytes (Moretti et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moretti et al., 2013

claim: iPSC-CMs can effectively model gene regulation in hearts from humans and chimpanzees.
source: we have shown that cardiomyocytes derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC-CMs) can effectively model gene regulation in hearts from humans and chimpanzees (Pavlovic et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pavlovic et al., 2018

claim: iPSC-CMs can be used to study CVD phenotypes including channelopathies such as long QT syndrome, and dilated cardiomyopathies such as Barth syndrome.
source: iPSC-CMs can be used to study CVD phenotypes including channelopathies such as long QT syndrome, and dilated cardiomyopathies such as Barth syndrome (Tanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2015

claim: Cardiomyocytes make up 70–85% of the heart volume.
source: Cardiomyocytes make up 70–85% of the heart volume, 30–40% of the total cellular composition (Pinto et al., 2016; Zhou and Pu, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pinto et al., 2016 and Zhou and Pu, 2016

claim: Cardiomyocytes make up 30–40% of the total cellular composition of the heart.
source: Cardiomyocytes make up 70–85% of the heart volume, 30–40% of the total cellular composition (Pinto et al., 2016; Zhou and Pu, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pinto et al., 2016 and Zhou and Pu, 2016

claim: Hypoxia induces a transcriptional response following stabilization of the HIF transcription factors under conditions of low oxygen.
source: Hypoxia induces a transcriptional response following stabilization of the HIF transcription factors under conditions of low oxygen (Samanta and Semenza, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samanta and Semenza, 2017

claim: Cardiomyocytes were differentiated from iPSCs of eight human and seven chimpanzee individuals.
source: We differentiated cardiomyocytes from iPSCs of eight human and seven chimpanzee individuals, including replicate differentiations from a subset of the lines (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Described in the methods and results sections

claim: Differentiated cells express the cardiomyocyte markers cardiac troponin T (TNNT2), sarcomeric alpha-actinin (ACTN1), and the ventricle-specific marker Iroquois Homeobox 4 (IRX4), in both species.
source: After 30 days in culture, differentiated cells, likely predominantly ventricular in subtype (Burridge et al., 2014), express the cardiomyocyte markers cardiac troponin T (TNNT2), sarcomeric alpha-actinin (ACTN1), and the ventricle-specific marker Iroquois Homeobox 4 (IRX4), in both species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: There is no difference in the median purity of the cardiomyocyte cultures between humans and chimpanzees.
source: Importantly, there is no difference in the median purity of the cardiomyocyte cultures between humans and chimpanzees (median purity in both species: 78%, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Transferring the cardiomyocytes from atmospheric oxygen levels (21% O2) to 10% O2 did not seem to induce stress in the cultures.
source: Transferring the cardiomyocytes from atmospheric oxygen levels (21% O2) to 10% O2 did not seem to induce stress in the cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by LDH activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: An increase in the level of 8-OHdG was observed following hypoxia and re-oxygenation in both species.
source: We observed an increase in the level of 8-OHdG following hypoxia and re-oxygenation in both species (BMean = 0.09 vs. CMean = 1.32; t-test; p=0.002 in chimpanzees, and BMean = −0.21 vs. CMean = 1.42; p=0.01 in humans; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by 8-OHdG measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A

claim: There is no difference in the amount of 8-OHdG released between species within a condition.
source: Within a condition, there is no difference in the amount of 8-OHdG released between species (human DMean = 1.19, chimpanzee DMean = 1.34).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of 8-OHdG data

claim: An increase in 8-iso-PGF2α release was found in chimpanzees following hypoxia.
source: We found an increase in 8-iso-PGF2α release in chimpanzees following hypoxia (AMean = 0 vs. BMean = 35.65; p=0.006), and a further increase following long-term re-oxygenation (DMean = 77.28; p=0.03; Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Supported by 8-iso-PGF2α measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B

claim: There is no significant increase in 8-iso-PGF2α release following hypoxia in humans.
source: While there is no difference in 8-iso-PGF2α release between species within any condition, we do not find a significant increase in 8-iso-PGF2α release following hypoxia in humans (AMean = 0 vs. BMean = 13.25; p=0.2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of 8-iso-PGF2α data

claim: 8-iso-PGF2α is known to be elevated in heart failure.
source: Nevertheless, our observations are intriguing because 8-iso-PGF2α is known to be elevated in heart failure (Mallat et al., 1998; Wolfram et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mallat et al., 1998 and Wolfram et al., 2005

claim: 8-iso-PGF2α is a risk marker for coronary heart disease.
source: and is a risk marker for coronary heart disease (Schwedhelm et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwedhelm et al., 2004

claim: ~4,000 genes respond to hypoxia at 10% FDR in each species.
source: Of 11,974 expressed genes, we identified ~4,000 genes that respond to hypoxia at 10% FDR in each species, and a slightly higher number of genes whose expression has changed upon re-oxygenation (Figure 2; the results of all tests are in Supplementary file 1-Table S3A).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: There is a strong correlation in the global gene expression response to both hypoxia and re-oxygenation in humans and chimpanzees.
source: Overall, there is a strong correlation in the global gene expression response to both hypoxia and re-oxygenation in humans and chimpanzees (median Spearman correlation = 0.78; sign test p<10−4 for all comparisons; Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: 147 genes responded to hypoxia in one species but showed little or no response in the other species, or responded in both species but showed the opposite direction of effect.
source: We identified 147 genes that responded to hypoxia in one species but showed little or no response in the other species, or that responded in both species but showed the opposite direction of effect (at FDR of 10%; Figure 4; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by species-by-condition interaction analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: 9,414 genes were categorized as not responding to hypoxia in either humans or chimpanzees.
source: Using this approach we categorized 9,414 genes as not responding to hypoxia in either humans or chimpanzees (non-response genes), 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species (conserved response genes), 430 genes that respond to hypoxia in chimpanzees only (chimpanzee-specific response genes), and 199 genes that respond to hypoxia only in humans (human-specific response genes; Figure 5 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian clustering analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: 1,920 genes respond to hypoxia in both species.
source: Using this approach we categorized 9,414 genes as not responding to hypoxia in either humans or chimpanzees (non-response genes), 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species (conserved response genes), 430 genes that respond to hypoxia in chimpanzees only (chimpanzee-specific response genes), and 199 genes that respond to hypoxia only in humans (human-specific response genes; Figure 5 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian clustering analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: 430 genes respond to hypoxia in chimpanzees only.
source: Using this approach we categorized 9,414 genes as not responding to hypoxia in either humans or chimpanzees (non-response genes), 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species (conserved response genes), 430 genes that respond to hypoxia in chimpanzees only (chimpanzee-specific response genes), and 199 genes that respond to hypoxia only in humans (human-specific response genes; Figure 5 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian clustering analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: 199 genes respond to hypoxia only in humans.
source: Using this approach we categorized 9,414 genes as not responding to hypoxia in either humans or chimpanzees (non-response genes), 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species (conserved response genes), 430 genes that respond to hypoxia in chimpanzees only (chimpanzee-specific response genes), and 199 genes that respond to hypoxia only in humans (human-specific response genes; Figure 5 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian clustering analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: HIF1α-bound regions and HIF2α-bound regions are enriched near conserved response genes compared to non-response genes.
source: Consistent with previous literature (Samanta and Semenza, 2017), the 356 HIF1α-bound regions, and 301 HIF2α-bound regions are enriched near conserved response genes compared to non-response genes (Chi-squared test; p<10−10 for both factors; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq integration analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Both HIF1α- and HIF2α-bound regions are enriched near conserved response genes compared to species-specific response genes.
source: We thus asked whether differences in HIF binding could account for inter-species gene expression differences. Indeed, both HIF1α- and HIF2α-bound regions are enriched near conserved response genes compared to species-specific response genes (p<0.01 for both factors; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq integration analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Chimpanzee-specific response genes are depleted for HIF binding.
source: In particular, chimpanzee-specific response genes are depleted for HIF binding (p<0.05 for both factors; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq integration analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Antisense transcripts are enriched in conserved response genes compared to non-response genes.
source: The 205 antisense transcripts are enriched in conserved response genes compared to non-response genes (49 vs. 142; p=0.001; Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by gene type analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: There is a significant enrichment in KEGG pathways related to the heart in the non-response gene category.
source: In the non-response gene category, there is a significant enrichment in KEGG pathways related to the heart (e.g. dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythymogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes, 10% FDR; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: There is a depletion of genes implicated in cardiovascular development and disease amongst the genes that respond to hypoxia in both species.
source: Indeed, we found that there is a depletion of genes implicated in cardiovascular development and disease amongst the genes that respond to hypoxia in both species (Chi-squared test; p=8.3×10−6; Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by cardiovascular gene analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: There is a depletion of eGenes in the conserved response category when compared to all expressed genes within each category, using data from the heart left ventricle.
source: We observe a depletion of eGenes in the conserved response category, when compared to all expressed genes within each category, using data from the heart left ventricle (Chi-squared test; p=0.01), heart right atrial appendage (p=1.4×10−5), and iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (p=6.4×10−5; Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by eQTL integration analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: The absolute effect size of eQTLs is significantly lower in the conserved response category compared to the non-response category.
source: This observation is further supported by the fact that the absolute effect size of eQTLs, measured by allelic fold change, is significantly lower in the conserved response category compared to the non-response category (p=0.001; Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by eQTL effect size analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: There is an enrichment of loss-of-function intolerant genes in the conserved response category.
source: When considering a set of 3,382 genes designated as loss-of-function intolerant in humans (Lek et al., 2016), we found that there is an enrichment of these genes in the conserved response category (p=0.02, Figure 7D; see Materials and methods), and depletion in the non-response category (p=0.005).
evidence: Supported by genetic tolerance analysis shown in Figure 7D

claim: A marginal yet significant increase in LDH activity was observed following hypoxia in humans.
source: We observed a marginal yet significant increase in LDH activity following hypoxia in humans, and a significant increase following short-term re-oxygenation in both species (Student's t-test; p<0.05; Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by LDH activity measurement data shown in Figure 8A

claim: A significant increase in LDH activity was observed following short-term re-oxygenation in both species.
source: We observed a marginal yet significant increase in LDH activity following hypoxia in humans, and a significant increase following short-term re-oxygenation in both species (Student's t-test; p<0.05; Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by LDH activity measurement data shown in Figure 8A

claim: TGFβ−1 release was significantly increased following re-oxygenation after hypoxic stress in both species.
source: We found that TGFβ−1 release was significantly increased following re-oxygenation after hypoxic stress in both species (p<7×10−3); however there is no difference between species under any condition (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by TGFβ−1 ELISA data shown in Figure 8B

claim: There is no difference in TGFβ−1 release between species under any condition.
source: We found that TGFβ−1 release was significantly increased following re-oxygenation after hypoxic stress in both species (p<7×10−3); however there is no difference between species under any condition (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by TGFβ−1 ELISA data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The expression of ~4,000 genes (about a third of all expressed genes) is altered following six hours of hypoxic stress in humans and chimpanzees.
source: We found that, in humans and chimpanzees, the expression of ~4,000 genes (about a third of all expressed genes) is altered following six hours of hypoxic stress.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis

claim: Many genes return to baseline expression levels within 24 hr of re-oxygenation.
source: Many of these genes return to baseline expression levels within 24 hr of re-oxygenation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential expression analysis across time points

claim: The response to hypoxia is highly conserved in humans and chimpanzees with 1,920 genes responding similarly.
source: The response to hypoxia is highly conserved in the two species with 1,920 genes responding similarly in humans and chimpanzees (75% of all genes that respond in at least one species).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian clustering analysis

claim: The conservation in response to hypoxia in this study is much greater than the conservation in immune response to infection between humans and chimpanzees.
source: There have not been many comparative studies of functional perturbations in primates to provide us with broad context, but the conservation in response to hypoxia in our study is much greater than the conservation in immune response to infection between humans and chimpanzees (Barreiro et al., 2010).
evidence: Comparison with results from Barreiro et al., 2010

claim: Genes responding to hypoxia are significantly depleted for known cardiovascular-associated genes.
source: However, genes responding to hypoxia are significantly depleted for known cardiovascular-associated genes, suggesting that hypoxic stress response genes are expressed, and active in multiple tissues.
evidence: Supported by cardiovascular gene enrichment analysis

claim: Conserved response genes are depleted for eGenes identified in the heart as well as in other tissues.
source: This is supported by the fact that we observe that conserved response genes are depleted for eGenes identified in the heart as well as in other tissues.
evidence: Supported by eQTL integration analysis across multiple tissues

claim: There is less tolerance for genetic variability that results in variation in the expression of genes that are necessary for eliciting a response to stress.
source: These results suggest that there is less tolerance for genetic variability that results in variation in the expression of genes that are necessary for eliciting a response to stress.
evidence: Inferred from the depletion of eGenes and enrichment of LoF intolerant genes in conserved response genes

claim: RASD1 is up-regulated specifically in humans following hypoxia.
source: Our most significant interaction corresponds to the RASD1 gene, which is up-regulated specifically in humans following hypoxia (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by species-by-condition interaction analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: LRRC25 responds to hypoxia specifically in chimpanzees.
source: Conversely, the LRRC25 gene responds to hypoxia specifically in chimpanzees, and has been found to inhibit NF-κβ signaling (Feng et al., 2017) (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by species-by-condition interaction analysis shown in Figure 4 and citation to Feng et al., 2017

claim: RASD1 was found to be up-regulated in samples from patients with ischemic disease compared to patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and non-failing hearts.
source: RASD1 was found to be up-regulated in samples from patients with ischemic disease compared to patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (heart damage despite normal blood flow), and non-failing hearts (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015

claim: The RAI1-PEMT-RASD1 region is a replicated, genome-wide significant locus for coronary artery disease (CAD).
source: The RAI1-PEMT-RASD1 region is a replicated, genome-wide significant locus for coronary artery disease (CAD) (McPherson and Tybjaerg-Hansen, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McPherson and Tybjaerg-Hansen, 2016

claim: The SNP in the RASD1-PEMT-RAI locus that is associated with CAD is not associated with various vascular-related traits.
source: The SNP in the RASD1-PEMT-RAI locus that is associated with CAD is not associated with various vascular-related traits (Schunkert et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schunkert et al., 2011

claim: The SNP in the RASD1-PEMT-RAI locus is associated with ischemic stroke, with the same direction of effect as CAD.
source: yet it is associated with ischemic stroke, with the same direction of effect (Dichgans et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dichgans et al., 2014

claim: The SNP in the RASD1-PEMT-RAI locus is an eQTL for RASD1 expression in monocytes.
source: Moreover, the SNP is an eQTL for RASD1 expression in monocytes (Emilsson et al., 2008; Schunkert et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Emilsson et al., 2008 and Schunkert et al., 2011

claim: The baseline level of DNA oxidation damage is similar in humans and chimpanzees.
source: The baseline level of DNA oxidation damage is similar in humans and chimpanzees, and increases following recovery from hypoxia in both species.
evidence: Supported by 8-OHdG measurement data

claim: DNA oxidation damage increases following recovery from hypoxia in both species.
source: The baseline level of DNA oxidation damage is similar in humans and chimpanzees, and increases following recovery from hypoxia in both species.
evidence: Supported by 8-OHdG measurement data

claim: The baseline level of lipid peroxidation is similar in humans and chimpanzees.
source: The baseline level of lipid peroxidation is also similar in humans and chimpanzees, and shows a trend towards increased levels during the course of the experiment in both species; however this increase is only significant in chimpanzees.
evidence: Supported by 8-iso-PGF2α measurement data

claim: Lipid peroxidation shows a trend towards increased levels during the course of the experiment in both species; however this increase is only significant in chimpanzees.
source: The baseline level of lipid peroxidation is also similar in humans and chimpanzees, and shows a trend towards increased levels during the course of the experiment in both species; however this increase is only significant in chimpanzees.
evidence: Supported by 8-iso-PGF2α measurement data

claim: There is no significant difference in the levels of 8-OHdG between humans and chimpanzees in blood samples.
source: These findings are in line with a study of oxidative stress markers in blood from ten male humans and ten male chimpanzees, which showed that there is no significant difference in the levels of 8-OHdG between species, but there is significantly elevated 8-iso-PGF2α levels in chimpanzees compared to humans (Videan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Videan et al., 2009

claim: There is significantly elevated 8-iso-PGF2α levels in chimpanzees compared to humans in blood samples.
source: These findings are in line with a study of oxidative stress markers in blood from ten male humans and ten male chimpanzees, which showed that there is no significant difference in the levels of 8-OHdG between species, but there is significantly elevated 8-iso-PGF2α levels in chimpanzees compared to humans (Videan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Videan et al., 2009

claim: The secreted metabolome is highly correlated between human and rhesus macaque cardiomyocytes after 24 hr of hypoxia.
source: Another comparative study on the effects of hypoxia in human and rhesus macaque cardiomyocytes demonstrates that the secreted metabolome is highly correlated between species after 24 hr of hypoxia (Zhao et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2018

claim: Out of 2,459 genes that respond to hypoxia in one or both species, only 371 (16%) were found to be differentially expressed between hearts and iPSC-CMs.
source: Out of 2,459 genes that respond to hypoxia in one or both species based on our data, only 371 (16%) were found to be differentially expressed between hearts and iPSC-CMs in Pavlovic et al.
evidence: Comparison with data from Pavlovic et al., 2018

claim: 34 of the 147 species-by-condition interaction genes (23%) were found to be differentially expressed between hearts and iPSC-CMs.
source: Similarly, 34 of the 147 species-by-condition interaction genes in our data (23%) were found to be differentially expressed between hearts and iPSC-CMs.
evidence: Comparison with data from Pavlovic et al., 2018

claim: Cardiomyocytes are more sensitive to superoxide radicals than cardiac fibroblasts.
source: Indeed, cardiomyocytes are more sensitive to superoxide radicals than cardiac fibroblasts (Li et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 1999

claim: The transcriptional response to hypoxia is generally conserved across species.
source: The transcriptional response to hypoxia is generally conserved across species, yet we were able to identify hundreds of species-specific regulatory responses including in genes previously associated with CVD.
evidence: Supported by the overall correlation analysis and differential expression results

claim: Hundreds of species-specific regulatory responses were identified including in genes previously associated with CVD.
source: The transcriptional response to hypoxia is generally conserved across species, yet we were able to identify hundreds of species-specific regulatory responses including in genes previously associated with CVD.
evidence: Supported by species-by-condition interaction analysis and Bayesian clustering

claim: The 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species are enriched for loss-of-function intolerant genes.
source: The 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species are enriched for loss-of-function intolerant genes; but are depleted for expression quantitative trait loci and cardiovascular-related genes.
evidence: Supported by genetic tolerance and eQTL integration analyses

claim: The 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species are depleted for expression quantitative trait loci.
source: The 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species are enriched for loss-of-function intolerant genes; but are depleted for expression quantitative trait loci and cardiovascular-related genes.
evidence: Supported by eQTL integration analysis

claim: The 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species are depleted for cardiovascular-related genes.
source: The 1,920 genes that respond to hypoxia in both species are enriched for loss-of-function intolerant genes; but are depleted for expression quantitative trait loci and cardiovascular-related genes.
evidence: Supported by cardiovascular gene enrichment analysis

claim: Response to hypoxic stress is highly conserved in humans and chimpanzees.
source: Our results indicate that response to hypoxic stress is highly conserved in humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the overall study results
